question: Events arrive in this order. Which (a, b) pairs does the EPL statement output?
code:
Events of four types arrive in this order (A1 is the first A event, B1 the first B event, and so on):

A1 C1 A2 B1 D1 A3 B2 C2 B3 C3 C4 A4 B4

select a, b
from pattern [every a=A -> b=B]
explanation: every restarts the A part per A: A1 and A2 both wait for a B, and B1 completes both waiters - one B can serve several waiters. A3 pairs with B2, and since B3 arrives before A4, A4 pairs with B4. Option 0 is what 'A -> every B' would output; option 3 is what 'every (A -> B)' outputs; option 1 is what the pattern without any every outputs.
hints: For every A that arrives, ask: which is the first B after it?
When B1 arrives, several waiters are open at the same time - which ones does it close?

question: Same event order, but a slightly different pattern. Which (a, b) pairs does the statement output?
code:
Events of four types arrive in this order (A1 is the first A event, B1 the first B event, and so on):

A1 C1 A2 B1 D1 A3 B2 C2 B3 C3 C4 A4 B4

select a, b
from pattern [A -> every b=B]
explanation: Here every binds to B: A matches once - the first A, A1 - and then every later B produces a new match with that same A. A2, A3 and A4 never take part, because the A side is never restarted. Option 1 is the result of 'every A -> B', and the last option has the order backwards: the arrow requires the B to arrive after the A.
hints: How many A events can take part at all, given where every sits?
A has already matched - what happens on every later B?

question: Now every wraps the whole sub-expression. Which (a, b) pairs does the statement output?
code:
Events of four types arrive in this order (A1 is the first A event, B1 the first B event, and so on):

A1 C1 A2 B1 D1 A3 B2 C2 B3 C3 C4 A4 B4

select a, b
from pattern [every (A -> B)]
explanation: every restarts the whole (A -> B) sub-expression only after a complete match. While the first instance waits for its B, A2 is ignored - the restart has not happened yet. After (A1,B1) the pattern waits for the next A: A3 pairs with B2, then A4 pairs with B4. Option 0 is 'every A -> B'; option 1 is 'A -> every B'; option 2 is the pattern without every.
hints: The pattern restarts only after a complete (A,B) match - what happens to an A that arrives while a B is still pending?
Trace it: which A is the first one to arrive after the (A1,B1) match?

question: Which statement correctly describes #length(7) and #length_batch(7) in Esper 8?
options: #length(7) keeps the last 7 events and is re-evaluated on every new event, while #length_batch(7) holds events until 7 have arrived and then releases them as one batch.
#length(7) releases events in fixed batches of 7, while #length_batch(7) slides forward one event per arrival.
Both keep every event that ever arrived; they differ only in how the output is sorted.
explanation: #length(7) is a sliding window: it always holds the most recent 7 events and the statement updates on every arrival. #length_batch(7) is a tumbling window: it collects 7 events, releases them together, and then empties. Option 1 swaps the two descriptions; both views bound what is kept, so the second-to-last option is wrong; both count events, so the last option is wrong.
hints: One of the two is sliding and the other tumbling - which is which?
Ask whether events stay in the window after it has been evaluated.

question: What does the every operator do in an Esper pattern?
options: It requires all events of the pattern to occur within the same second.
It restarts the sub-expression it applies to after each of its matches, so the pattern can match again and again.
It changes the followed-by operator so the events may arrive in any order.
It makes the pattern fire once on the first complete match and then stop.
explanation: every is a repetition operator: after the sub-expression it applies to has matched, it restarts that part, so the pattern can fire repeatedly. Option 4 describes exactly the opposite - the behavior of a pattern without any every, which matches only once. Options 0 and 3 describe things every does not do.
hints: What happens after a pattern without every has matched once?
Where every is placed decides which part of the pattern gets repeated.
